prompt: Write a ~700-word piece of literary short fiction about: a weather forecaster in a town where she is always wrong. Prose only, no headings.
text:
Elena stood before the three towering monitors that dominated her small office on the second floor of the municipal building, their blue light washing over pale features and casting long shadows against the beige walls. Outside the frosted glass window, a gentle gray mist clung to the cobblestones of Oakhaven, promising another day of drizzle that would likely turn into sleet by afternoon if she was lucky—or unlucky enough for her patterns to hold true. But luck had never been on Elena's side in this town; it seemed fate itself viewed Oakhaven as a testing ground for every law of meteorology except the one regarding reliability.

She adjusted the collar of her cardigan, smoothed an imaginary wrinkle from her forecast sheet, and took a deep breath that smelled faintly of stale coffee and ozone. Today's prediction was straightforward: high pressure system moving in from the west, temperatures hovering around fifty degrees, clear skies by evening with perhaps a dusting of snow flurries before midnight. It sounded simple enough for any child to guess, yet Elena knew better than anyone how easily simplicity unraveled when she stepped into the role of authority here.

"Good morning," she said automatically as three heads popped up from their desks in the break room area behind her glass partition. "Anybody got a strong wind chill warning?" she added with forced cheerfulness.

Mrs. Gable, who had lost count of how many times Elena predicted sunshine while Mrs. Gable's husband slipped on ice patches under his own porch umbrella yesterday, merely shrugged. "Don't hold your breath," she murmured. She knew better than anyone that in Oakhaven, the weather was a malicious puzzle designed specifically to thwart Elena's calculations.

She walked out onto the street for her morning coffee run, passing a group of children building snowmen despite it being forty degrees and sunny—a scenario she had explicitly ruled out just hours ago based on satellite imagery showing warm fronts colliding with cold pockets higher than usual. The irony tasted bitter in her mouth as she sipped her lukewarm brew while standing under the awning that offered no protection from a sudden burst of hail five minutes later, which left perfect white craters across the parking lot and dented Mrs. Gable's sedan.

By noon, Elena retreated back to her office where the real work began: updating models after every unexpected twist in atmospheric pressure or unseasonal gusts that defied all logic. Every time she updated the forecast board outside with a marker, someone would glance up at it and immediately point out how wrong last week's prediction had been—how clear skies turned into monsoon-like downpours within an hour of her saying "partly cloudy." The town held onto every error like sacred talismans, preserving them in memory banks where they could be accessed whenever Elena needed to feel small beneath the weight of their collective skepticism.

Yet there was something strangely compelling about this dance between prediction and impossibility. In Oakhaven, accuracy wasn't just difficult; it felt impossible because nature itself seemed determined to mock her expertise day after day after day. Perhaps that's why she stayed so long despite offers from larger cities with better equipment and more forgiving atmospheres where predictions were taken seriously rather than laughed off or used as punchlines at dinner parties.

As evening approached, the sky outside began shifting hues of violet and charcoal gray, hinting at storm clouds gathering faster than her models suggested. Yet even then, Elena couldn't shake off a strange sense of resignation mixed with curiosity about what twist would come next: Would rain fall? Or would snow begin falling while everyone laughed hysterically over how wrong she was again? She watched the barometer drop steadily and prepared herself for yet another round of corrections that would inevitably follow tomorrow morning when someone else pointed out how perfectly predictable her mistakes had become in this peculiar little town where nothing ever went according to plan but everything somehow worked itself into a strange kind of rhythm all its own.
topic: a weather forecaster in a town where she is always wrong
